A.explanation: Too small by a factor of about 16. It gives a charge of only about $0.005 \text{ C}$, not the $0.0800 \text{ C}$ transferred in $4.00 \text{ s}$.

B.explanation: Too small by a factor of 4. It is the number of electrons for $1.00 \text{ s}$ of current, since $Q = It = 0.0200 \text{ C}$ for $1.00 \text{ s}$.

C.explanation: Current $I = 0.0200 \text{ A}$ for $4.00 \text{ s}$ gives $Q = 0.0800 \text{ C}$, which is $0.0800/e = 5.00 \times 10^{17}$ electrons.

D.explanation: Far too large. It mistakes the magnitude of the elementary charge, giving about $10^4$ times too many electrons for $0.0800 \text{ C}$.

hints: Notice the given $200 \, \Omega$, $4.00 \, \text{V}$ and $4.00 \, \text{s}$ - first find the current from p.d. and resistance.
Connect current to charge with $Q = It$, then connect charge to electron count with $Q = Ne$.
Calculate $I = 4.00/200$, then $Q$, then divide $Q$ by $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C}$ to get $N$.
walkthrough: Find the current in the $200 \, \Omega$ resistor using $I = V/R$. Here $I = 4.00/200 = 0.0200 \, \text{A}$.
Find the charge entering the resistor in $4.00 \, \text{s}$ using $Q = It$. So $Q = 0.0200 \times 4.00 = 0.0800 \, \text{C}$.
Relate total charge to number of electrons using $Q = Ne$, where $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \, \text{C}$ is the elementary charge.
